newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Tough times still ahead for Brazil banks in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Tough times still ahead for Brazil banks in 1997.

text.p: Brazilian banks, still reeling from a two-year stabilization drive that eliminated easy arbitrage profits, will have to cut staff and administrative costs to make it through another tight year, analysts and bankers said.

"Lower spreads will lead to further cost cuts this year, forcing banks to reduce personnel and redesign their branch network," said Antonio Carlos Castrucci, president of the Brazilian Association of Commercial and Universal Banks (ABBC) and head of Banco Paulista.

Analysts said there was room for cuts in staff expenses, which account for around 70 percent of total banking costs. A study by Austin Asis consulting firm on last year's nine-month results of 90 banks showed that personnel costs rose 16 percent to $6.5 billion over the same period of 1995.
The study covers Brazil's largest banks such as Bradesco, Banco Itau and Banco Real, but excludes federal government bank Banco do Brasil, which has posted heavy losses over the past two years.

Cost-cutting is aimed at bolstering bank earnings, which at the 90 banks fell slightly to $1.7 billion in the first nine months of 1996, down from $1.8 billion in the same year-ago period. Last year banks derived most of their profits from a reduction in income tax, the sale of discounted housing debt to the federal government and earnings from subsidiaries and stock holdings. But analysts say banks cannot depend on these non-banking profits this year.
"Banks will no longer be able to rely on these artificial tools. They will have to profit from banking activities," said Erivelto Rodrigues, an analyst at Austin Asis.
Staff costs in local banks represent 2.3 percent of their assets, much higher than in other countries, he said.
"Banks will have to learn to do the same or more with less employees," Rodrigues said.

Brazilian banks have been going through a brutal transformation since the Real stabilization Plan slashed the country's once sky-high inflation to single digits, forcing them to cut costs, join forces through mergers and acquisitions and secure market niches.

Analysts said revenues from loans have been shrinking as a result of a combination of lower spreads and slow lending growth due to a high level of consumer and corporate defaults over the past two years.

Total revenues at the 90 banks examined by Austin Asis totalled $30 billion between January and September 1996, of which $17.6 billion or 58 percent came from loans. In the same period of 1995, loans accounted for $16.8 billion or 70 percent of $23.4 billion in total revenues.
The banking sector is also expected to see more mergers and acquistions in 1997, especially among medium-sized banks which must strengthen to stay in business, experts said.
"Banks in the world tend to seek scale. This also has to happen here," said Carlos Daniel Coradi, from EFC Consultores & Associados.
Last year the biggest merger deals involved private banks BCN and Banco Itamarati, and Banco Excel, which took over failed bank Banco Economico.
